subject: physics_2
question_text: Derive an expression for the intensity of the electric field at a point on the axial line of an electric dipole.

mark_split.label: Fields at P due to +q and −q

verification.note: The 1+1+1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. For this Physics-II paper the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers. Hand-checked: (r+a)² − (r−a)² = 4ra and (r−a)²(r+a)² = (r²−a²)², so E = (q/4πε₀)·4ra/(r²−a²)² = (1/4πε₀)·2pr/(r²−a²)²; for r ≫ a this becomes (1/4πε₀)·2p/r³, directed along p. CORRECTED FROM THE BOOK (printed p.20): the book's intermediate line reads 'E_axial = q/4πε₀ · (2a)(q)·r/(r²−a²)²', which carries the charge q twice and drops the factor 2 — the correct grouping is q·4ra = 2(q·2a)r = 2pr, and the book's own next line, 2Pr/4πε₀(r²−a²)², is right, so the slip is confined to that one intermediate line. The book writes the dipole moment as capital P; the standard lowercase p is used here, matching the other cards of this chapter. The book prints 'seperated' and 'neglisible'; both are written correctly here.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.label: The dipole and the point P
steps.mark_note: p = q × 2a, and P at a distance r
lines: Consider an electric dipole with charges −q
and +q separated by a distance 2a, with its
centre at O. Its dipole moment is
directed from −q to +q. Let P be a point on
the axial line at a distance r from O, on
steps.margin_note: First mark. Name q, 2a, p, r and the point P before any field is written.
steps.why: The result is written in p and r, so both must be defined first: p from the charge and the separation, r from the centre O out to the point P on the axis.
common_mistakes: Writing p = q × a. The separation of the charges is 2a, so p = q × 2a.
Measuring r from one charge. It is measured from the centre O.

recall.must_convey: That a dipole of charges −q and +q separated by 2a has moment p = q × 2a, and P lies on the axis a distance r from the centre O.
accept: charges minus q and plus q separated by 2a
point P on the axial line at distance r from the centre
reject: one by four pi epsilon nought two p by r cubed

steps.memory_tip: Define the dipole first: two charges, separation 2a, moment p = q × 2a.

steps.label: The figure
steps.margin_note: The charges −q and +q on the axial line, the dashed distance r from the centre of the dipole out to P, and the two fields at P drawn above the line: E₁ due to +q pointing outwards, E₂ due to −q pointing back.
steps.why: The figure fixes the two distances the derivation needs — (r − a) from +q and (r + a) from −q — and shows that the two fields at P lie along one line in opposite directions, which is why they subtract.
common_mistakes: Drawing both field arrows the same way. At an axial point they are opposite.
Marking r from +q. r is measured from the centre O of the dipole.

recall.must_convey: That the figure shows the dipole about O, P on the axis at a distance r, and the two opposite field arrows at P.
accept: draw the dipole and mark P on the axis
show the two field arrows at P in opposite directions
reject: E equals E one minus E two

steps.memory_tip: Charges on a line, P further out, two arrows at P facing opposite ways.

steps.label: Fields at P due to each charge
steps.mark_note: E₁ and E₂ with the correct distances
lines: P is at a distance (r − a) from +q and
(r + a) from −q. The field at P due to +q is
directed away from the dipole, and the field
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Both fields written with the correct distance, and each with its direction.
steps.why: Each charge sets up its own field at P and the two add as vectors. On the axis they lie along one line, so only the two distances (r − a) and (r + a) and the two directions are needed.
common_mistakes: Using r for both distances. P is nearer +q by a and further from −q by a.
Writing (r − a)² as r² − a². They are not the same.

recall.must_convey: That E₁ = (1/4πε₀)q/(r − a)² away from the dipole and E₂ = (1/4πε₀)q/(r + a)² towards it.
accept: q by r minus a whole squared
q by r plus a whole squared
the two fields are in opposite directions
reject: two p r by r squared minus a squared whole squared

steps.memory_tip: Nearer charge, smaller denominator: (r − a) belongs to +q.

steps.label: Resultant field at P
lines: E₁ is larger than E₂, so the resultant field
at P acts along p. Its magnitude is
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Subtract, take the common denominator, then group q × 2a into p.
steps.why: The two fields are opposite, so the resultant is their difference. Over the common denominator (r² − a²)² the numerator becomes (r + a)² − (r − a)² = 4ra, and q × 2a is exactly p, so 4raq becomes 2pr.
common_mistakes: Adding E₁ and E₂. They are opposite, so they subtract.
Leaving the answer in q and a. Group q × 2a into the dipole moment p.

recall.must_convey: That E = E₁ − E₂ simplifies to (1/4πε₀)·2pr/(r² − a²)².
accept: four r a over r squared minus a squared whole squared
two p r by four pi epsilon nought into r squared minus a squared whole squared

steps.memory_tip: Difference of two squares on top: (r + a)² − (r − a)² = 4ra.

steps.label: Short dipole result
lines: For a short dipole a is much smaller than r,
so a² can be neglected and (r² − a²)² ≈ r⁴.
The field is along p, that is from −q to +q.
steps.margin_note: Last mark. State the short dipole condition, simplify, then give the direction.
steps.why: Exam work uses the short dipole, where a² is small next to r². Dropping it turns (r² − a²)² into r⁴ and leaves the inverse cube law every dipole field obeys.
common_mistakes: Writing 1/r². A dipole field falls off as 1/r³, not as 1/r².
Leaving out the direction. On the axial line E is along p.

recall.must_convey: That for r ≫ a, E = (1/4πε₀)·2p/r³, directed along p.
accept: a is much less than r
two p by four pi epsilon nought r cubed
the field is along the dipole moment
reject: four r a over r squared minus a squared whole squared

steps.memory_tip: Axial field carries the 2: 2p on the axis, plain p on the equator.

insider_note: The axial field is twice the equatorial field at the same distance — carrying the 2 on the axis and dropping it on the equator is the fastest way to keep the two derivations apart.
